title: Your First HTML File (Without VS Code)

sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

You're going to write a real webpage from scratch using nothing but Notepad. No frameworks, no tutorials, no dependencies — just a text file and a browser. By the end you'll have a working webpage that you built yourself, an understanding of the most essential HTML tags, and a feel for how the edit-save-refresh cycle works. Every website on the internet starts exactly like this.

## HTML Is Just a Text File Here's the thing most people don't realise about websites: at the bottom of every webpage — from a simple blog to a complex web app — is a plain text file with a `.html` extension. The browser reads that file and renders it visually. That's it. HTML (HyperText Markup Language) uses **tags** — labels wrapped in angle brackets `< >` — to describe the *structure* of a document. The browser reads those tags and knows: "this is a heading," "this is a paragraph," "this is an image." A tag works like this: `

` opens a heading, `

` closes it. Everything between the opening and closing tags is the content. The `/` before the name signals a closing tag: ```html

This is a heading

This is a paragraph.

This is a link ``` This pattern — open tag, content, close tag — is the foundation of all HTML. Once you understand it, reading someone else's HTML becomes natural.

## The Minimum Valid HTML File Every HTML file has the same basic skeleton: ```html Page Title

Hello, world!

This is my first webpage.

``` Let's read every line: **``** — Tells the browser "this is an HTML5 document." Required at the top of every HTML file. Not technically a tag — it's a declaration. **`` and ``** — The root element. Everything on the page lives inside these. **`` and ``** — Contains information *about* the page that isn't shown directly: the page title, links to stylesheets, metadata. The browser reads it, but visitors don't see it. **`Page Title`** — The text that appears in the browser tab. **`` and ``** — Everything inside `` is what the user *sees*. This is where all your content goes. **`

Hello, world!

`** — Level-1 heading. The largest heading. There are six levels: `

` through `

`. **`

This is my first webpage.

`** — A paragraph of text. The indentation (spaces before tags) is for human readability only — the browser ignores it. But consistent indentation is a universal developer habit because it makes the structure obvious at a glance.

## The Essential HTML Tags You don't need to memorise every HTML tag — there are over 100. But these 15 cover everything you'll need for basic web pages: **Text and headings:** ```html

Largest heading

Second level heading

Third level heading

A paragraph of text.

Bold text Italic text
``` **Links and images:** ```html Click here About page (relative link) ``` **Lists:** ```html
  • Unordered list item (bullet points)
  • Another item
  1. Ordered list item (numbered)
  2. Second item
``` **Structure and style:** ```html
A generic container (block element)
Inline container for text styling
``` **The `style` attribute (quick inline CSS):** ```html

Blue heading

Styled paragraph

``` The `style` attribute lets you add CSS directly to an element without a separate stylesheet. Not the best practice for large projects, but perfect for learning and quick experiments.

**The Notepad trap:** When you save a file in Notepad, it defaults to saving as `.txt`. If you name your file `hello.html` but the 'Save as type' dropdown is still 'Text Documents (*.txt)', Windows saves it as `hello.html.txt` — and the browser won't open it as a webpage. **Always change 'Save as type' to 'All Files (*.*)'** when saving HTML files in Notepad. Then type the full filename including `.html` in the filename box.

## How to Open Your File in a Browser

Once you've saved `hello.html`, no server or hosting is required to view it locally:

1. Open File Explorer
2. Navigate to where you saved the file
3. Double-click `hello.html`

Your default browser opens and displays the page. The address bar will show `file:///C:/Users/.../hello.html` — that's a local file URL. It works entirely on your computer.

**The edit-save-refresh cycle:**
1. Make a change in Notepad
2. Press `Ctrl+S` to save
3. Switch to the browser and press `F5` to refresh
4. See your change

This cycle — edit, save, refresh — is the fundamental loop of all web development. Professional developers using React, Vue, or any modern framework are doing essentially the same thing with more automation around step 3.

sections.title: Hello Web — Build a Styled Personal Page
sections.content:
You're going to build a real webpage about yourself with headings, paragraphs, a list, and basic styling. Follow every step. **Step 1 — Open Notepad:** Press the Windows key, type `notepad`, press Enter. **Step 2 — Type your HTML:** Type the following, replacing all `[placeholder]` text with your own content: ```html About [Your Name]

[Your Name]

Learning AI Tools & Code

About Me

I'm currently [describe what you do or are learning in one sentence].

What I'm Learning

  • AI tools and how to use them effectively
  • [One thing you want to learn from this course]
  • [Another skill or topic you're interested in]

A Quote I Like

"[Write your favourite quote here]"

Built with HTML on [today's date].

``` **Step 3 — Save correctly:** 1. Click **File** → **Save As** 2. Navigate to `Documents\ai-course-projects\exercises` 3. Change **'Save as type'** dropdown to **'All Files (*.*)'** 4. In the **'File name'** field, type exactly: `hello.html` 5. Click **Save** **Step 4 — Open in your browser:** 1. Open File Explorer 2. Navigate to `Documents\ai-course-projects\exercises` 3. Double-click `hello.html` You should see your styled page: dark blue heading, grey subtitle, sections, a bulleted list, and italicised quote. **Step 5 — Make a change:** 1. Go back to Notepad 2. Find the ``, add: ```html

Useful Link

Go to Claude.ai

``` Save and refresh. Click the link to test it. **Step 7 — Add an image (optional):** If you have any photo saved on your computer, copy it into your `exercises` folder and add: ```html ``` **Reflection:** Open `notes/html-notes.md` and write: - What tag structure confused you most? - What did the `style` attribute let you do? - What would you need to learn to turn this into a real website?

sections.question: You've built an HTML page in Notepad, saved it, and opened it in the browser. You make a change to the HTML — but after pressing F5 in the browser, nothing changes. What is the most likely cause?
options: The browser has cached the old version and can't be refreshed
You edited the HTML but forgot to save the file in Notepad before refreshing the browser
HTML files can't be updated after they're opened in a browser
The file extension was wrong — it was saved as .txt instead of .html
sections.explanation: The browser always reads the file from disk when you press F5 — but it reads whatever is currently saved on disk. If you made changes in Notepad but didn't press Ctrl+S before pressing F5 in the browser, the browser refreshed the old saved version. The edit-save-refresh cycle requires saving first. This is the single most common mistake beginners make when editing HTML in Notepad. The solution: always save (Ctrl+S in Notepad) before refreshing (F5 in browser).

sections.title: Workshop A — Add a Page to Your HTML File
sections.content:
This drill extends the HTML file you created in the lesson — turning it into a real two-page site. **Step 1 — Open your index.html** from the lesson in a text editor (Notepad or VS Code). **Step 2 — Add a new page.** Create a second file called `about.html` in the same folder with this structure: ```html About — My First Site

About This Site

Write a sentence about yourself or this project here.

Back to Home ``` **Step 3 — Link the pages together.** In index.html, add a link to about.html: ```html About ``` **Step 4 — Test it.** Open index.html in a browser. Click your new link. Does it navigate to about.html? **Step 5 — Ask Claude:** *"I have an index.html and about.html that link to each other. What are the next 3 things I should add to make this look like a real website?"*

sections.title: Workshop B — AI-Built Web Page for a Real Use Case
sections.content:
Use AI to build a real HTML page you will actually use — not a practice exercise.

**Step 1 — Choose a real purpose** for a web page: a personal portfolio, a project landing page, a cheat sheet, an event invitation, a simple dashboard.

**Step 2 — Describe it to Claude:**
```
I want to create a single HTML page (no frameworks, just plain HTML and inline CSS) for: [describe your use case]

It should include:
- [list the sections you want]
- [any specific content]
- [any styling preferences — colours, fonts, layout]

Make it look professional. Include all the HTML in one complete file I can save and open in a browser.
```

**Step 3 — Save the HTML** Claude gives you to a file and open it in a browser.

**Step 4 — Request targeted improvements:**
- "The header looks too plain — make it have a coloured background"
- "Add a contact section at the bottom"
- "Make it work better on mobile"

**Step 5 — Mandatory review:** Ask Claude: *"Review this HTML you just wrote. Find 3 specific problems: accessibility issues, layout problems on small screens, or missing elements that a professional web developer would add."* Fix at least 2 issues.

**Step 6 — This page is yours.** Keep it and show it to someone.

sections.title: Workshop C — HTML Debugging with AI
sections.content:
When HTML breaks, knowing how to get AI to fix it is more valuable than knowing every HTML tag. **Step 1 — Intentionally break your HTML** by removing a closing tag (remove `

` or ``) or by making a typo in a link (`href` → `hrf`). **Step 2 — Open the broken file in a browser.** How does it look? Does the browser show an error or just silently break the layout? **Step 3 — Paste the broken HTML to Claude** and ask: *"This HTML isn't rendering correctly. Find all the errors and fix them. Explain what each error was and why it caused the problem it did."* **Step 4 — Compare** Claude's fixed version to your original. Did Claude find the error you introduced? Did it find any other issues? **Step 5 — Use browser DevTools:** Press F12 in your browser. Click the Elements tab. This shows you the actual HTML the browser is rendering — different from what you wrote if there are errors. **Step 6 — Learn the rule:** Right-click any element on any webpage → Inspect Element. You can see the HTML of any website. This is how web developers learn — by reading real HTML from real sites.

sections.title: Workshop D — Add CSS Styling to Your Site
sections.content:
Your HTML site works — now make it look good. CSS controls appearance: colours, fonts, layout, spacing.

**Step 1 — Open index.html** in a text editor.

**Step 2 — Ask Claude to add professional styling:**
```
I have this HTML file: [paste it]

Add CSS styling to make it look professional. Requirements:
- A clean, modern font (use Google Fonts or system fonts)
- A colour scheme with a primary and secondary colour
- Proper spacing and margins
- The links should look like buttons, not plain text
- It should look good on both desktop and mobile

Add all CSS inside a <style> tag in the <head>. Give me the complete updated file.
```

**Step 3 — Save and open** the updated file. Does it look how you wanted?

**Step 4 — Make one specific change** yourself: find the colour code in the CSS (like `#3498db`) and change it to a different colour. See the effect immediately by refreshing the browser.

**Step 5 — Share your finished site** with someone — even just as a screenshot. You built a real webpage.

options: A file was not saved properly
A tag that was opened with <tag> was never closed with </tag>, causing the browser to not know where the element ends
The browser doesn't support this HTML version

sections.question: What is the difference between HTML and CSS?
options: HTML is for websites, CSS is for apps
HTML defines the content and structure (what is on the page); CSS defines the appearance (how it looks)
HTML is older and CSS replaced it
They are two names for the same technology
sections.explanation: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) defines structure and content — headings, paragraphs, links, images, lists. CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls visual presentation — colours, fonts, spacing, layout, animations. They work together: HTML is the skeleton, CSS is the skin and clothing. You can change a page's entire visual design by changing only CSS, without touching the HTML content.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 4-6.** You understand how files are organized, you can navigate the terminal with confidence, you know what code is and how errors work, and you've built and opened your first styled webpage. Next: lesson 4-7 extends these foundations further.

**Across industries:**

- **HR/People Ops:** an HR coordinator builds a styled onboarding page — benefits, contacts, first-week checklist — that new hires open in any browser, no company software required.
- **Government/Public Sector:** a records clerk publishes a plain HTML page of office hours and permit requirements that loads instantly on any device, including an old phone.
- **Manufacturing & Operations:** a floor supervisor posts a one-page HTML safety-procedure reference on shop-floor tablets, editable in Notepad mid-shift.
- **Nonprofit & Social Impact:** a volunteer coordinator hand-codes an event page with schedule and sign-up link instead of paying for a website builder.
- **Retail & Hospitality:** a shop owner builds a bare-bones page with hours, menu, and directions that loads fast and costs nothing to host.
